## The pairings

| Block | For |
| --- | --- |
| **LUT** | any boolean function of its inputs |
| **Flip-flop** | one bit of state, clocked |
| **BRAM** | dense on-chip memory |
| **DSP slice** | hardened multiply-accumulate |
| **BUFG** | distributing a clock with balanced delay |

The spare description is an **IO buffer** (an IOB), which handles the pad, the voltage standard, the drive strength and often a serialiser. It matters enormously in practice and is not part of the logic fabric.

## The LUT is the idea that makes an FPGA an FPGA

A 6-input LUT is 64 bits of configuration memory and a 64-to-1 multiplexer. Load the truth table you want and it computes that function. Any function of six inputs — AND, XOR, a 6-bit parity, one bit of an adder, an arbitrary piece of control logic — is the *same hardware* with different bits loaded.

That is the whole trick: an FPGA does not contain gates that get wired together, it contains tables that get filled in. "Configuring" an FPGA means writing those tables and the routing switches between them, which is why the configuration is a bitstream rather than a program and why it is held in SRAM that must be reloaded at power-up.

Resource counts are quoted in LUTs for this reason, and the figure to have a feel for is that a small 32-bit RISC-V core is a few thousand LUTs.

## Why BRAM and DSP exist at all

Both could be built from LUTs and flip-flops. Both would be ruinous.

**Memory.** One bit in a flip-flop costs a flip-flop and a share of the routing around it. A 36 Kbit BRAM costs one block. Building 36 Kbit from registers would consume thousands of cells and route terribly. So FPGAs include a few hundred to a few thousand BRAMs, and **running out of BRAM is one of the two most common ways a design fails to fit**. Noticing that your buffer is 20% too big for the available BRAM is a design-time problem, not a debugging one.

**Multipliers.** A 25x18 multiplier built from LUTs is hundreds of cells and a long critical path. A DSP slice does it in one block, at a far higher clock rate, with an accumulator attached. For filters, FFTs, matrix arithmetic and neural-network inference the DSP count *is* the performance ceiling — it is the figure quoted as an FPGA's "throughput", and the reason DSP-heavy designs are mapped carefully rather than left to the tools.

The general lesson: the fabric is general-purpose, and the hardened blocks are where the vendor decided generality was not worth its cost. Knowing which blocks are scarce tells you which part of your design the tools will struggle with.

## The clock buffer is the one people skip

A clock has to arrive at every flip-flop at almost the same time. Route it through ordinary fabric and the delay to a flop at one corner differs from the delay to a flop at the other by more than a clock period at any useful frequency — and then the design simply does not work, in a way that is nearly impossible to debug from a waveform.

So FPGAs have dedicated clock trees with buffers designed for low **skew**, and there are only a handful of them. Two consequences for real designs:

- **Put clocks on clock resources.** Deriving a clock with ordinary logic — gating it with an AND, or using the output of a flip-flop as a clock — is the classic beginner mistake. The tools warn about it; the warning is not optional. Use a clock enable on the flip-flops instead.
- **Clock domain crossings need synchronisers.** A signal moving between two unrelated clocks will eventually be sampled mid-transition, and metastability propagates. Two flip-flops in series on the receiving clock is the minimum; an asynchronous FIFO is the right answer for buses.
